lessons.title: Exam Technique: Media Language and Representation Paper
lessons.content_html:
Structuring Your Answers on the First Paper

Exploring the Media is worth 40% of your final grade and is split into two sections. Section A tests media language and representation through print media forms such as magazines, film posters, newspapers and print advertisements. Section B tests media industries and audiences through film, newspapers, radio and video games. Knowing exactly how many marks each question carries — and which command word it uses — is the fastest way to control your timing and hit every band.

Every question is built around a command word. The command word tells you which skill the mark scheme rewards: an ‘analyse’ question answered only with description cannot reach the top bands, no matter how much detail is included.

Key Fact

Section A carries 45 marks: Question 1 (15 marks, media language), Question 2(a) (5 marks, context) and Question 2(b) (25 marks, extended comparison). Section B carries 35 marks across two stepped questions on industries and audiences.

Question 1: Analysing Media Language (15 marks)

Question 1 assesses media language in relation to one set product and is stepped, so the earlier parts may use command words such as ‘identify’ or ‘explain’ before the highest-tariff part asks you to analyse how media language constructs meaning. Reference to relevant contexts may also be required. This means explaining what choices the producer made and why those choices construct particular meanings — not simply naming the techniques you can see.

Noticing that a magazine cover uses a close-up shot is only the starting point. A higher-band answer explains what that close-up connotes — intimacy, accessibility, emotional appeal — and links it to the wider meaning the whole cover constructs for its target audience.

A common mistake is feature-spotting: listing everything you can see (colour, font, image, headline) without explaining its effect. The higher bands are awarded for explaining the effect of a feature, not for noting that it is present. For every feature you name, add a ‘because’ — because this constructs a particular representation, or because this appeals to a specific audience.

Question 2(a): Explaining Context (5 marks)

Question 2(a) asks you to explain context of production in relation to one set product. This is worth only 5 marks, so a tight, focused answer that links context directly to a specific feature of the product is far stronger than a general history lesson about the period.

Key Fact

A common error is treating context as an add-on: describing the historical period and then separately describing the product, with no connection between the two. A secure context answer always shows how a specific choice in the product reflects the time, society or politics in which it was made.

Question 2(b): The Extended Comparison (25 marks)

Question 2(b) is the single largest question on the first paper. You compare a set product with an unseen resource in the same media form, using comparative connectives throughout, not just in an introduction or conclusion.

The weakest comparative answers write two separate blocks: one paragraph entirely about the set product, then one paragraph entirely about the unseen resource, with no comparison between them. The strongest answers interweave both products in every paragraph, using connectives such as ‘whereas’, ‘similarly’ and ‘in contrast’ to build a genuinely comparative argument about how each product constructs meaning.

Section B: Stepped Questions on Industries and Audiences

Section B uses stepped questions on two of the media forms you have studied. One question assesses media industries; the other may assess media industries, audiences or media contexts, so you must revise all three areas for every Section B form. Each stepped question moves from short, low-tariff parts testing recall towards longer parts requiring explanation and application to the set product.

A crucial rule applies here: the Section B set products (such as a newspaper, a radio programme, a film franchise website or a video game) are studied as examples of industry and audience issues, so detail about a product’s camerawork, layout or colour scheme only helps if it supports an industry, audience or context point — the focus here is ownership, funding, regulation, targeting and audience response.

Uses and gratifications theory (associated with Blumler and Katz) is named in the specification content for audiences, so it is legitimate to use. Listing the four needs (information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, and entertainment) is not enough on its own — apply one of them to a named set product and explain how the product satisfies it. Simply listing the four needs (information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, and entertainment) without applying them to a specific product will not reach the higher bands. The strongest answers explain how a named set product actually satisfies one of these needs for its audience.

Use the set products to illustrate industry and audience concepts, not to analyse their content. Discussing how a video game website uses interactive features to reach a mass audience is valid; describing the colour scheme of its homepage is not, unless it directly illustrates an industry or audience point such as branding across platforms.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Underline the command word in every question before you start writing. ‘Analyse’ needs explanation of effect and meaning, not a list of features. ‘Compare’ needs both products discussed together in every paragraph, not two separate mini-essays. For the 25-mark comparison, spend the first minute planning matching points across both products so your comparative connectives have something to link.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Section A (45 marks) covers media language, context and an extended comparison; Section B (35 marks) covers stepped questions on industries and audiences.
  • Analyse effect, not just presence — and keep the unseen resource genuinely compared throughout Question 2(b), never treated in a separate block.
  • Section B set products are used to illustrate media industries, audiences and media contexts — keep textual detail only where it supports an industry, audience or context point.

practice_questions.text: Identify one command word used in Question 1 on the first paper.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly names a precise command word from Question 1, such as 'analyse'.
Secure: Names a command word that broadly matches the question type.
Developing: Names a related term that is not itself a command word.
Emerging: Vague or unrelated answer such as 'write about' with no command word identified.

practice_questions.text: State one way a media producer uses selection, and one way they use exclusion, when constructing a newspaper front page.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both selection and exclusion are stated with a clear, specific example for each.
Secure: Both are stated but one example lacks detail or precision.
Developing: Only one of the two concepts is stated with a valid example.
Emerging: Selection and exclusion are confused or no valid example is given for either.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which a media organisation's ownership might affect how a product reaches its target audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two ways clearly explained with developed reasoning linking ownership to audience reach, using accurate terminology.
Secure: Two ways explained with relevant reasoning, though development may be uneven.
Developing: One way explained clearly, or two ways stated with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about ownership with little link to audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the social context of a print advertisement you have studied is reflected in its use of imagery or language.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise link between a specific social context and a specific feature of the advertisement, clearly explained.
Secure: A relevant link between context and the advertisement, explained with some detail.
Developing: Context and advertisement both mentioned but the link between them is unclear or one-sided.
Emerging: Description of context or advertisement alone, with no genuine connection made.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the selection and combination of image, headline and colour construct meaning on the front cover of a magazine you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated analysis of how selection and combination construct specific meanings, using precise terminology and embedded evidence throughout.
Secure: Clear analysis of how features construct meaning, with relevant terminology and evidence.
Developing: Some analysis attempted, but tends towards feature-spotting with limited explanation of effect.
Emerging: Features are named or described with little or no explanation of meaning.

practice_questions.text: Compare how a film poster you have studied and an unseen film poster in the same form each construct representations of their central character, using comparative connectives throughout your response.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained, genuinely comparative argument using connectives throughout, with sophisticated analysis of representation in both posters and a substantiated conclusion.
Secure: Clear comparison with connectives used regularly, relevant evidence from both posters and a reasonable conclusion.
Developing: Some comparison attempted but the response drifts into separate blocks on each poster for parts of the answer.
Emerging: The two posters are described in separate sections with little or no direct comparison.

knowledge_checks.q: Which command word is used in Question 1 on the first paper?
How many marks is the extended comparison question (Question 2(b)) worth on the first paper?
A _____ question in Section B moves from short recall parts to longer explanation parts.
In Question 2(b), you must compare a set product with an _____ resource in the same media form.

right: 25 marks — compare with an unseen resource

glossary_terms.definition: The word in a question that tells you what skill to demonstrate, such as analyse, explain or compare.
The forms, codes and conventions media producers use to create and communicate meaning, including selection, combination and exclusion of elements.
The historical, social, cultural or political circumstances surrounding when and how a media product was produced, and how these circumstances shape it.
A previously unstudied media product given to you in the exam for analysis, always in the same media form as one of the set products.
Linking words and phrases such as whereas, similarly and in contrast that show a comparison is being made between two products.
A question broken into linked parts that build in mark tariff, usually moving from short recall to extended explanation.

lessons.title: Exam Technique: Television and Music Paper
lessons.content_html:
Command Words for the Television and Music Paper

The second written paper tests everything you know about television and music in depth. It is worth 30% of your final grade and carries 60 marks across two sections: Section A on television and Section B on music, including music video and online media. Because this paper draws on all four areas of the theoretical framework — media language, representation, media industries and audiences — the strongest answers link these areas together rather than treating them as separate boxes to tick.

An answer that links these areas together is often called a joined-up or connected response: for example, explaining how a broadcaster's decision to air a programme on a particular channel (industry) shapes the kind of representation it can show (representation) and who is likely to watch it (audience). Learning to make these connections is the single most useful exam technique skill for this paper.

Key Fact

Section A (Television) is worth 30 marks. Question 1 (20 marks) has two parts analysing media language or representation in the set extract. Question 2 (10 marks) tests media industries, audiences or media contexts.

Answering the Television Extract Question

Before the extract is shown, you get two minutes to read the Section A questions. The extract itself runs for about three minutes and is played twice, with a six-minute gap in between for making notes. Use that gap well: note down specific camera shots, editing choices, dialogue and elements of mise-en-scène you can name precisely, because vague description (“the camera moves around”) scores far lower than a precise one (“a low-angle shot positions the detective as powerful before the reveal”).

Question 1 (20 marks) is split into two parts and always focuses on either media language or representation in the extract — never both at once. Part (a) asks you to analyse the extract, so you must explain how techniques create meaning, not just identify them. Part (b) asks you to make judgements and draw conclusions, which means building an argument about how effective, typical or significant those techniques are — reference to relevant contexts may also be required here.

Question 2 (10 marks) moves away from the extract itself to test your knowledge of media industries, audiences or media contexts connected to the set television option you studied — for example how a programme’s broadcaster and funding model shaped its production, or how it targets and is consumed by its intended audience.

A common mistake is describing what happens in the extract — retelling the plot, listing camera shots — without ever reaching a judgement. Making a judgement means taking a position: is this representation typical of the genre or does it challenge convention? Is this use of editing highly effective at building tension, or only partially successful?

Drawing a conclusion means pulling your points together into a final, substantiated view, rather than trailing off after your last example. A strong closing sentence might state clearly how the extract, taken as a whole, positions the audience or constructs its central representation, tying every earlier point back to that single argument.

Key Fact

Section B (Music) is worth 30 marks. Question 3 (20 marks) analyses media language or representation in the set music products through judgements and conclusions, and may require reference to relevant contexts. Question 4 (10 marks) tests media industries, audiences or media contexts.

Answering the Music Question

Question 3 asks you to make judgements and draw conclusions about media language or representation in the set music video and website. Unlike the television question, it is not split into two parts — you build the full 20-mark judgement in a single extended response, so your answer needs a clear structure from the start: an opening line of argument, developed points with named examples, and a conclusion that answers the question directly.

Question 4 tests media industries, audiences or media contexts connected to the music topic. This could mean explaining how streaming and social media have changed how artists reach audiences, or how an artist’s website and social platforms work together to build a brand identity.

Blumler and Katz’s Uses and Gratifications theory argues audiences are active, not passive: they choose media to satisfy specific needs. Simply naming the four needs — information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, and entertainment — is not enough on its own: the criteria reward applying them to the set product.

The higher marks come from applying the theory to the actual set product. Instead of writing “audiences use media for personal identity,” write something like: “fans of the artist may use the official website’s behind-the-scenes content to build a sense of personal identity, feeling connected to the artist’s persona and values.” Naming the need and then explaining exactly how the specific product meets it is what separates a basic answer from a good one.

Getting Context and Representation Working Together

Whenever a question allows reference to relevant contexts, treat context as evidence for your argument, not a fact bolted on at the end. Instead of finishing a paragraph with a stray sentence like “this reflects the time it was made,” explain the link directly: how does a particular representation, camera technique or piece of dialogue reflect the historical, social, cultural or political circumstances the product was made in?

It is tempting to treat every stereotype in a television extract or music video as simply harmful. A stronger argument is a balanced one: stereotypes also let audiences interpret media quickly, because a familiar shorthand communicates character or setting fast, and stereotypes can change over time as social attitudes shift.

A strong answer might argue that a representation relies on a recognisable stereotype for speed and clarity, before considering whether it also reinforces a narrow or outdated view of the group being represented. Showing both sides of this argument, rather than a single-note complaint, produces the substantiated judgement the 20-mark questions ask for.

Key Fact

The four areas of the theoretical framework — media language, representation, media industries and audiences — are tested together on this paper. Linking them, rather than treating each in isolation, is what the higher-mark bands reward.

Both sections on this paper reward the same underlying skill: moving beyond description to a substantiated argument. Whether you are analysing a three-minute television extract or a music video and its website, plan your judgement before you start writing, choose precise named examples, and finish with a conclusion that directly answers the question set.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Time yourself against the marks: the paper gives you about a minute and a half per mark, so allow roughly 30 minutes for each 20-mark judgement question and about 15 minutes for each 10-mark question, including a few minutes to plan before you write. When a question says “make judgements and draw conclusions,” never stop at describing what you see — state clearly what you think the extract or product achieves and why, using named examples throughout. When context is allowed, always tie it back to a specific technique or representation rather than mentioning it as a separate, disconnected fact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Section A (Television) is 30 marks: Q1 (20 marks, two parts on media language or representation in the extract) and Q2 (10 marks, industries/audiences/contexts).
  • Section B (Music) is 30 marks: Q3 (20 marks, single judgement on media language or representation) and Q4 (10 marks, industries/audiences/contexts).
  • Always move from description to a substantiated judgement, apply theory like Uses and Gratifications to the named product, and treat stereotypes and context as two-sided arguments woven through the evidence.

practice_questions.text: Name the original broadcaster of the 1970s crime drama studied for comparison with the contemporary crime drama option.
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: ITV. Any other answer scores no marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain how differences in funding model between a 1970s crime drama extract and a contemporary crime drama extract might be reflected in their content and style.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated, explicit link between funding model and specific stylistic or content choices, using named examples from both extracts. Secure: Clear link between funding context and general stylistic choices, with at least one example. Developing: Some awareness that context affects style, but examples are limited or vague. Emerging: Simple, unlinked statement about funding or context with no connection to the product.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an artist's official website and their use of social and participatory media might work together to target and engage a young audience for a new song release.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed explanation of how website and social platforms combine to build audience engagement, referencing specific features and audience needs. Secure: Clear explanation of how website and social media work together, with relevant detail. Developing: Some explanation of website or social media use, but the link between them is underdeveloped. Emerging: Basic or generic statement about websites or social media with little explanation.

practice_questions.text: A contemporary music video opens with a slow-motion shot of the artist looking directly at the camera before cutting to a fast-paced dance sequence. Make a judgement about how effective this combination of camerawork and editing is in engaging a young audience.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Confident, substantiated judgement about effectiveness, analysing both camerawork and editing with precise terminology. Secure: Clear judgement supported by relevant analysis of camerawork and editing. Developing: A judgement is attempted but analysis of technique is limited or one-sided. Emerging: Description of the shots with little or no judgement reached.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how camera angles and editing are used in a television crime drama extract to construct the detective character as authoritative.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, detailed analysis of specific camera angles and editing choices, explaining precisely how each constructs authority. Secure: Clear analysis of camera angles and editing with relevant explanation of meaning. Developing: Some identification of techniques with partial explanation of effect. Emerging: Techniques are named but not analysed for meaning.

practice_questions.text: Analyse and draw conclusions about how a music video from the 1980s and a contemporary music video use representation differently to construct the identity of the artist.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, comparative argument with detailed evidence from both videos, ending in a substantiated conclusion about differing representation. Secure: Clear comparison with relevant evidence from both videos and a stated conclusion. Developing: Some comparison attempted but underdeveloped, or conclusion is weak. Emerging: Description of one or both videos with little comparison or conclusion.

A command word requiring detailed examination of how specific media language techniques create meaning, rather than simply listing what is present.

lessons.title: Creating Media Products: The Non-Exam Assessment
lessons.content_html:
Creating Media Products: The Non-Exam Assessment

The final part of your course is not a written exam. It is a non-exam assessment (NEA) — a single media production that you plan, create and submit yourself, marked by your teacher and checked by external moderators. It is worth 30% of your final grade and carries 60 marks in total.

Unlike the two written papers, this piece of work only assesses AO3. Every mark you earn comes from what you can make, not what you can write about someone else’s product. But the theory you learned for the written exams — media language, representation, audience — is exactly what you apply here.

Key Fact

The non-exam assessment is worth 60 marks and 30% of the qualification. It assesses AO3 only — applying knowledge of media language and representation to create a production for a specific audience.

Choosing a Production Brief

New production briefs are set every year, always across the same four fixed media forms: television, magazines, advertising and marketing for film, and advertising and marketing for music. Each brief always states the target audience you must design for, along with the required genre or style. Briefs are published on 1 March, the year before assessment, giving candidates time to plan carefully rather than rush into production.

Television: create a sequence from a new television programme, or a website to promote one. Advertising and Marketing (Music): create a music video, or a website to promote a new artist or band. Advertising and Marketing (Film): create print-based marketing material for a new film. Magazines: create a new print or online magazine. Whichever brief you choose, every task it sets must be completed within roughly twelve weeks of research, planning and production.

The Statement of Aims

Before submitting your production, you must write a statement of aims. This is roughly 250 words explaining how your production applies media language and representation, and how it targets its audience. It is compulsory: if you do not submit a production, you are awarded zero marks for the statement of aims too.

Key Fact

The statement of aims is approximately 250 words and is worth 10 of the 60 marks available for the non-exam assessment.

Research and Planning

Before you film, design or record anything, you carry out research and planning. Neither is marked separately, but both shape the quality of the final production, so they matter enormously. Research includes analysing similar media products to identify their codes and conventions, and finding out how real products target their audiences. Planning includes producing a pitch or treatment, a project timeline, and documents suited to your chosen form — a shot list, storyboard, script or draft designs.

Research is about understanding what already exists: studying how similar products use media language, and finding out what audiences expect from that genre or form. Planning is about preparing your own production: deciding shots, writing scripts, sketching layouts, and scheduling your twelve weeks of work. Your teacher must be able to see and authenticate both stages, even though neither is directly marked.

Using Original Material

Every image, piece of footage and line of text in your production must be your own original material — you cannot use an existing brand, an existing magazine title, or footage you did not shoot yourself. This rule is central to the assessment: a candidate who does not use original footage, images or text cannot be awarded marks above band 2 for the production, whatever else the work achieves.

There is one exception. For a music video, you may use an existing song by a real artist, as long as that song does not already have an official music video. Any non-original music used as a soundtrack must be copyright-free and acknowledged on your cover sheet.

Key Fact

You may use an existing song for a music video, provided it has no existing official video, and you credit it on the cover sheet. Everything else must be your own original work.

How the Production Is Assessed

The 60 marks split three ways. Ten marks reward your statement of aims. Twenty marks reward how fully your production meets the requirements of the brief — completing every task, suiting the specified form and genre, and being appropriate for the target audience. Thirty marks, the largest single share, reward how well you use media language to communicate meaning and construct representations, for example through camerawork, layout, editing or the way people and places are portrayed.

The strongest productions do more than tick boxes: they use techniques with purpose, control connotations deliberately, and build representations that stay consistent and convincing across the whole piece, rather than appearing only in places.

Support, Supervision and Deadlines

Because this is coursework, strict rules govern how much help your teacher can give. Teachers can explain the brief and the marking criteria, and give general advice on what needs improving once work is underway. What they cannot do is tell you exactly how to fix a specific problem, give detailed advice on how to appeal to your audience, or hand you a writing frame for the statement of aims — the work must remain genuinely yours.

Key Fact

Work is authenticated at three stages: when planning is completed, at a suitable point during production (for example once footage or a full draft exists), and when the production is finished.

The whole process — aims, research and planning, and production — must be completed within around twelve weeks, so that no single project takes over your entire course. Plan your time early: the production stage always takes longer than you expect.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When you write your statement of aims, name the actual techniques you plan to use — which camera angles, colour schemes or codes of representation you intend to include — rather than describing your idea in vague terms. Markers reward specific, subject-terminology-rich statements that show real understanding of media language and representation, not just a summary of what your production is about.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The non-exam assessment is worth 30% of your grade (60 marks) and assesses AO3 only — creating a production, not writing about one.
  • Your statement of aims (about 250 words, 10 marks) must explain how you will apply media language and representation to reach your target audience.
  • All material must be original except an existing song without an official video; using non-original material caps your marks at band 2.

practice_questions.text: Name the assessment objective that the non-exam assessment (Creating Media Products) solely assesses.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correctly names AO3 (creating media products for an intended audience by applying knowledge and understanding of the theoretical framework to communicate meaning). Secure: Names AO3 without full detail. Developing: Names the wrong AO but shows some awareness of the framework. Emerging: No creditable response given.

practice_questions.text: State two items a candidate must submit for their non-exam assessment production to be assessed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both items stated accurately with detail, e.g. the completed media production and the statement of aims (or completed cover sheet). Secure: Two valid items stated with limited detail. Developing: One valid item stated. Emerging: Vague, incorrect or missing response.

practice_questions.text: Explain briefly why the statement of aims cannot earn any marks if a candidate does not submit a production.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clearly explains that the statement of aims is only assessed alongside the finished production, and no production means an automatic zero for both elements. Secure: Explains the link between production and statement of aims with minor gaps. Developing: Basic or partial explanation. Emerging: States a fact without explaining the link.

practice_questions.text: Explain how researching the social and cultural context of real magazines aimed at young adults could inform a candidate's planning decisions for a magazine production brief.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains, with specific examples, how understanding real magazines' conventions, values and audience appeal directly shapes decisions on layout, cover lines, imagery and tone. Secure: Explains a clear link between context research and planning choices with some detail. Developing: General points about researching magazines with limited link to planning. Emerging: Describes magazines with no clear link to context or planning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how understanding audience targeting could shape the choices a candidate makes when creating a website to promote a new television programme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated explanation linking audience targeting theory to specific website design choices (images, language, interactive features) that would appeal to and engage the stated target audience. Secure: Clear explanation of how audience targeting influences at least two website design choices. Developing: Basic explanation with limited application to the brief. Emerging: General comments about audiences with little or no link to website choices.

practice_questions.text: With reference to the marking criteria for the non-exam assessment, explain what separates a production that excellently meets the requirements of its set brief from one that only partially meets it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, well-structured explanation covering completion of all brief tasks, consistent use of relevant conventions, and an appropriate mode of address for the target audience, contrasted clearly with partial completion, inconsistent conventions and a less appropriate mode of address. Secure: Clear explanation of several relevant contrasts between excellent and partial brief fulfilment. Developing: Some relevant points made but underdeveloped or one-sided. Emerging: Simple, general statement with little reference to the marking criteria.

knowledge_checks.q: What percentage of the qualification does the non-exam assessment make up?
Which of these is NOT one of the four fixed media forms for non-exam assessment briefs?
The statement of aims is approximately _____ words long.
A candidate who does not use original footage, images or text cannot be awarded marks above band _____ for the production.
Match each mark allocation to what it assesses in the non-exam assessment.
right: Meeting the requirements of the set brief
Using media language to communicate meaning and construct representations

glossary_terms.definition: Assessment Objective 3: creating media products for an intended audience by applying knowledge and understanding of the theoretical framework to communicate meaning.
The specific group of people a media product is designed to appeal to and engage, defined by factors such as age, interests or lifestyle.
A compulsory written outline, of about 250 words, explaining how a candidate's production will apply media language and representation and reach its intended audience.
Content created entirely by the candidate rather than taken from an existing source, brand or product.
